question.text: Using the Rule of 72, approximately how many years will it take for an investment to double at an annual return of 9%?

explanation.text: The Logic: The Rule of 72 is a standard rule-of-thumb in personal finance: the approximate number of years for an investment to double at a constant annual return is 72 divided by the percentage rate of return. At a 9% annual return, doubling time is approximately 72 / 9 = 8 years. The precise compound-interest doubling time at 9% is about 8.04 years, so the rule gives a very close approximation here. The Trap: 6, 7 and 9 years all correspond to misapplying the formula (e.g., using 60/r, 70/r or 72/8 instead of 72/9), or to confusing the rule with the more precise log-based doubling formula. Note: The Rule of 72 shortcut is not stated on the cited pages of the NISM-Series-X-A Investment Adviser (Level 1) workbook, which on the pages checked supports general compounding (FV/PV) formulas rather than the 72/r doubling shortcut. The framing above is general personal-finance / time-value-of-money knowledge.
